extracted.subtask_description: Use the JOSS reviewer checklist to evaluate a software submission's repository, functionality, documentation, development practices, and paper sections; confirm COI and adherence to the code of conduct. This is the checklist-driven review workflow for the Journal of Open Source Software.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist completion (procedural)
rubrics_metrics.description: JOSS reviews are checklist-driven. A JOSS review is generally considered incomplete until the reviewer has checked off all of their checkboxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should work through the checklist for each submission and not consider the review complete until every item is checked off. Consult the review criteria page to better understand how checklist items should be interpreted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: I confirm that I have read the JOSS conflict of interest policy and that: I have no COIs with reviewing this work or that any perceived COIs have been waived by JOSS for the purpose of this review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers must declare any conflicts or ensure they have been waived per the JOSS COI policy before proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Code of Conduct adherence
rubrics_metrics.description: I confirm that I read and will adhere to the JOSS code of conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers must behave according to the journal's code of conduct while interacting with authors and editors during the review process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repository availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the source code for this software available at the repository url?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify the repository URL in the submission points to the actual source code. The code should be accessible (not private/removed) and correspond to the submitted work.

rubrics_metrics.name: License file presence and type
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the repository contain a plain-text LICENSE file with the contents of an OSI approved software license?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for a plain-text LICENSE file at repository root and confirm the license is OSI-approved. If no license or non-OSI license is present, flag this as an issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution and authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Has the submitting author made major contributions to the software? Does the full list of paper authors seem appropriate and complete?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether authorship accurately reflects major contributors and that the submitting author legitimately represents the project. Look for any missing or inappropriately included authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and significance (high-level)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does this submission demonstrate clear research impact or credible scholarly significance as described in the JOSS guidelines?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the software makes a clear, defensible scholarly contribution per JOSS guidance (e.g., new capability, enabling research, broadly useful). If unclear, request clarification or justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Development timeline (sustained development)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the project show evidence of sustained development over time (preferably months or years) rather than rapid, recent code generation?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for commit history, releases, and activity over a prolonged period; very recent single-author repositories with little history should be scrutinized for sustainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open development (public history and engagement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Was the software developed openly from early stages? For projects with recent public repositories, is there at least six months of public development history with evidence of releases, public issues/pull requests, and ideally external engagement?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer projects with a public development record (issues, PRs, releases). For newly public repos, expect ≈6 months of activity and signs of community interaction where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative effort / community engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the project show evidence of community engagement such as contributions from multiple developers, issues/discussions from external users, or community influence on the development described in the paper?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check contributors list, pull requests from external users, issues opened by others, discussions, and evidence that the community influences direction. Single-developer projects are acceptable but should be represented honestly in the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good open-source practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the project follow good open-source practices (license, documentation, tests and/or verification processes, releases, and clear contribution/support pathways)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify presence of license, README, contribution guidelines, tests, release/versioning, and clear issue/support reporting mechanisms. Note missing or inadequate practices as review comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Installation (functionality checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does installation proceed as outlined in the documentation?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the installation instructions as written and confirm they work. Note missing steps, incorrect dependency specifications, or platform-specific issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional claims verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Have the functional claims of the software been confirmed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test the software to confirm it performs as described in the paper and documentation (basic end-to-end usage). If claims are not verifiable from provided examples, request reproducible examples or fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance claims verification
rubrics_metrics.description: If there are any performance claims of the software, have they been confirmed? (If there are no claims, please check off this item.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If authors assert performance characteristics (speed, memory), attempt to reproduce benchmarks or verify methodology; if none claimed, mark as not applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation: statement of need (docs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do the authors clearly state what problems the software is designed to solve and who the target audience is?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The README/paper should clearly explain the problem domain and target users. If this is ambiguous, request clarification in docs and paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation: installation instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Is there a clearly-stated list of dependencies? Ideally these should be handled with an automated package management solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependencies should be explicit (requirements files, setup metadata) and installation should preferably work via package managers (pip, conda, etc.). Note missing dependency declarations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation: example usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Do the authors include examples of how to use the software (ideally to solve real-world analysis problems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for worked examples, tutorials, or notebooks demonstrating typical use-cases. Examples should be runnable and relevant to intended users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation: functionality documentation (API)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the core functionality of the software documented to a satisfactory level (e.g., API method documentation)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for API reference, docstrings, or user guides that explain the main functions/classes and their parameters, return values, and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation: automated tests or verification steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there automated tests or manual steps described so that the functionality of the software can be verified?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer automated test suites (unit/integration) and/or documented manual verification steps. Ensure tests are runnable and indicate coverage of core functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation: community guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there clear guidelines for third parties wishing to 1) Contribute to the software 2) Report issues or problems with the software 3) Seek support
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for CONTRIBUTING.md, issue templates, code of conduct for contributors, and information on how to request help or report bugs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software paper: Summary (required section)
rubrics_metrics.description: Has a clear description of the high-level functionality and purpose of the software for a diverse, non-specialist audience been provided?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper's summary must communicate what the software does in accessible language for non-specialists. If overly technical or vague, request revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software paper: Statement of need (required section)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the paper have a section titled ‘Statement of need’ that clearly states what problems the software is designed to solve, who the target audience is, and its relation to other work?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper must include a named 'Statement of need' section describing problem, audience, and how this tool fits into or differs from existing options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software paper: State of the field (required section)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the paper include a “state of the field” section that describes how this software compares to other commonly-used packages? If related tools exist, do they provide a clear “build vs. contribute” justification explaining their unique scholarly contribution and why alternatives are insufficient?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should compare to existing tools and justify why their software is needed (build vs contribute). Verify comparisons are fair and referenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software paper: Software design (required section)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the paper include a “software design” section that explains the trade-offs weighed, the design/architecture chosen, and why it matters? Is the content compelling and does it demonstrate meaningful design thinking?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The design section should explain architecture decisions and trade-offs; it should be substantive and show thoughtful engineering relevant to the problem domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software paper: Research impact statement (required section)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the paper include a “research impact statement” section providing evidence of realized impact (publications, external use, integrations) or credible near-term significance (benchmarks, reproducible materials, community-readiness signals)? Is the evidence presented compelling?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect concrete evidence of impact (citations, users, integrations) or plausible near-term plans and benchmarks. Assess the persuasiveness of the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software paper: AI usage disclosure (required section)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the paper include an “AI usage disclosure” section that transparently discloses any use of generative AI in the software creation, documentation, or paper authoring?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must declare any use of generative AI; reviewers should check for this section and that disclosures are transparent and complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software paper: Quality of writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the paper well written (i.e., it does not require editing for structure, language, or writing quality)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess clarity, structure, grammar, and readability. If the paper requires substantive editing, request revisions before acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software paper: References completeness and citation syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the list of references complete, and is everything cited appropriately that should be cited (e.g., papers, datasets, software)? Do references in the text use the proper citation syntax?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify references include related work, datasets, and software as appropriate and that in-text citations follow JOSS citation syntax. Flag missing or incorrect citations.
